frameworks.name: The Ladder Rung Model
frameworks.definition: Focus requires consolidating all available effort into a single endeavor until critical mass is achieved; spreading effort across multiple projects prevents any from reaching the threshold for success.

frameworks.name: The 10-Stage Roadmap (Zero to $100M+)
frameworks.definition: A predictable progression of business stages indexed by headcount, with each stage carrying distinct constraints and symptoms; graduation requires removing the constraint via documented steps.

claims.text: Productivity comes from all the things that you choose not to do, not things you add. Focus means doing fewer things outside the primary objective—it is the antithesis of adding productivity hacks.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Commitment is the elimination of alternatives. Like marriage, commitment reduces optionality and forces depth over breadth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: In the extreme, focus means doing literally one thing—eating and sleeping are necessary maintenance, but everything else is noise. The most focused person says no to the maximum number of activities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Environmental distractions—windows overlooking streets, knock-able doors, Slack notifications, people passing by—prevent focus because they are not the work itself. Removing environmental noise is a prerequisite for focused output.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Distractions interrupt the mental model required for deep work, forcing re-entry costs.

claims.text: When a person works on the same project continuously for 20 years, accumulating 20 years of deliberate practice, they become expert-level regardless of the project domain. The object is to get 20 years of practice in one thing, not to optimize project selection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: 20+ year commitment to a single domain
claims.mechanism: Repeated reps compound skill; domain choice is irrelevant to output quality given sufficient time. Expertise emerges from duration and focus, not inherent talent.

numbers.axis: years of practice in one domain

bounded_by: Does not apply to domains with rapid exogenous change (e.g., regulatory regimes, technology platforms) where 20-year static focus can become obsolete

claims.text: The fallacy of multi-project pursuit is that spreading effort across three or four opportunities will identify which one works; in reality, any of them would work if one received the consolidated effort that is being split.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Success requires crossing a minimum effort threshold per project. Splitting effort below-threshold across multiple projects guarantees all fail, whereas consolidating effort into one project allows threshold-crossing.
bounded_by: Assumes projects are substitutable in effort requirement (not applicable to serial projects with hard timing constraints)

claims.text: A founder with a profitable business (50% gross margin, high revenue retention, strong customer acquisition and delivery capability) identified their constraint as themselves—their impulse to start new projects rather than deepening the existing one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: The hard part of plan execution is not creating the plan or following it—it is sticking with the plan across time. Plan failure is typically attributed to poor planning, but the true failure is founder discipline to remain on the plan.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Founder discipline/boredom is the binding constraint for plan success, not plan quality. Poor stickiness yields plan abandonment regardless of plan caliber.

claims.text: This progression—zero to $100M+ across 10 stages indexed by headcount, with documented constraints and graduation steps—has been replicated by Hormozi across software, physical products, service businesses, and brick-and-mortar, establishing the stages as category-agnostic.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: all business categories tested: software, physical products, services, brick-and-mortar
less than 1% of companies complete all 10 stages

numbers.axis: company completion rate of 10-stage roadmap to $100M+

examples.text: A founder in cybersecurity had built a business with 50% margins, strong revenue retention, high customer acquisition capability, and excellent delivery—all non-constraint functions. When asked what was wrong, he identified himself as the constraint: his tendency to get bored and start new projects rather than deepen the existing one. Hormozi's response was that if the founder committed 20 years to the existing business (accumulating 20 years of reps in one domain), he would become extraordinarily good at it, making the boredom impulse—his desire to explore new opportunities—the bottleneck to further scaling.

Hormozi uses a ladder-rung metaphor: imagine a wall you must climb. You have materials to build four rungs, but placing all four rungs against the wall separately creates only a short ladder. The mistake is assuming you can do all four rungs (or opportunities) simultaneously and 'see which one works.' Instead, you take all four rung-materials and consolidate them into a single ladder tall enough to clear the wall. By taking the second rung's material and adding it to the first, then the third and fourth, you create one tall ladder that clears the wall and reaches the other side—where 'all the money and happiness' reside. This illustrates that any single project would work if given consolidated effort, but none work with split effort.

practices.text: Eliminate environmental distractions from your workspace: close windows that create visual distraction, prevent people from casually knocking on your door, disable Slack notifications, and remove uncontrolled foot traffic—anything that is not the work itself.

When facing multiple promising projects, consolidate all effort into one project until it reaches critical mass (evidence of traction, product-market fit, or revenue milestone). Only after that single project is self-sustaining should you consider starting a second one.

Access the 10-stage roadmap from zero to $100M+ at acquisition.com/roadmap by entering your information; it details each stage's constraints, symptoms, and graduation steps across eight business functions.
